query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Uniform Cu-shell plating on W powder prior to consolidation will raise the room-temperature thermal conductivity of a 50 vol % W–Cu composite by ≥20 % while leaving compressive strength (≥500 MPa) and post-irradiation conductivity retention (loss ≤10 % after 0.1 dpa at 500 °C) comparable to or better than an otherwise identical composite made from uncoated W powder.
generation.material_initial_state: Blend of commercially pure W powder (1–10 µm) and atomised Cu powder sized to give a nominal 50 vol % W–Cu composition; powders contain <100 ppm O and no intentional surface treatments.
generation.intervention: Electroless Cu plating that deposits a continuous 0.5–1 µm Cu shell on each W particle before spark-plasma sintering (SPS).
generation.conditions: Composite fabricated by SPS at 1000 °C, 50 MPa, 10 min in vacuum; service temperature ≤800 °C under inert or vacuum environment and neutron doses up to 0.1 dpa (14 MeV equivalent).
generation.structural_mediator: The Cu shell eliminates W–Cu interfacial porosity, produces a continuous Cu network upon sintering, and forms coherent/semi-coherent W|Cu interfaces that act as efficient phonon/electron pathways and defect-recombination sinks.
generation.mechanism:
1. Thermal: Reduced Kapitza resistance and higher effective Cu-network connectivity lower phonon/electron scattering.
2. Mechanical: Metallurgical bonding across the Cu shell improves load transfer and suppresses interfacial crack initiation.
3. Irradiation: Semi-coherent interfaces serve as sinks that recombine point defects, limiting radiation-induced void swelling and associated conductivity loss.
generation.predicted_outcome: Laser-flash measurements will show ≥270 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 25 °C (vs. ≈225 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ for the baseline); compressive yield strength ≥500 MPa; after 0.1 dpa/500 °C irradiation, conductivity drop ≤10 % (still ≥15 % higher than baseline).
generation.baseline: An SPS-consolidated 50 vol % W–Cu composite produced from the same powders without Cu shell plating.
generation.boundary: Effect expected for 30–70 vol % W, Cu-shell thickness 0.3–2 µm, and operating T ≤0.6·T_m(Cu) (~800 °C). Benefit diminishes if Cu network becomes discontinuous (porosity >2 %) or if shell is non-uniform >10 % thickness variation.
generation.uncertainty: Long-term stability of the very thin Cu shell under prolonged thermal cycling and high-dose (>0.1 dpa) neutron exposure is not yet verified; plating uniformity may vary with particle morphology.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of 50 vol % W–Cu samples by SPS: (A) with Cu-plated W powder (0.7 µm shell) and (B) uncoated W powder. Measure density (Archimedes), microstructure (SEM/EBSD), and baseline thermal conductivity (laser-flash, 25–800 °C) and compressive strength (RT). Irradiate half of each set with 1.8 MeV He⁺/W⁺ ions to 0.1 dpa at 500 °C, then re-measure conductivity and perform TEM for defect characterization.
measurements: TEM defect density at W|Cu interface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If sample A shows <15 % improvement in initial thermal conductivity over sample B OR loses its conductivity advantage (<5 % higher than B) after irradiation, the hypothesis is falsified.
